title: Capacity-proxy routing guardrails for Dedicated-to-Hosted escalation
creator: Aisha Khatri
description:
Problem:
Teams are seeing unpredictable cost and customer impact during capacity pressure events when traffic is automatically escalated from Dedicated pools into Hosted. Current behavior lacks tenant-aware throttles, per-tenant burst accounting, and model-variant quality gates — leading to surprise latency regressions, quota overruns, and noisy neighbor incidents.

Goal:
Design and implement a set of guardrails (capacity-proxy) in the routing layer that: 1) enforce tenant-level burst budgets and decay rules, 2) select safe target regions/tiers during escalation, and 3) pick fallback model variants by quality/latency profile rather than naively routing to the cheapest available instance. The system should preserve SLOs where possible and provide clear observability and opt-out controls for customers.

Proposed design (high level):
- Capacity-proxy scoring engine: runtime component that scores candidate routes using a multi-factor vector: Dedicated pool health, tenant burst budget, regional latency delta, cost delta, and model-variant quality delta. Score thresholds determine whether escalation is allowed, throttled, or denied.
- Tenant burst accounting: per-tenant token bucket (burst credits) with configurable decay windows. Credits are consumed on escalation; credits can be purchased or configured via Dedicated contracts.
- Region selection policy: prefer same-region hosted routes when within acceptable latency delta (+X ms), otherwise evaluate cross-region routes with weighted penalty. Policies are pluggable by customer and by org defaults (e.g., prefer low-cost regions for non-PHI tenants).
- Tier routing rules: respect committed Dedicated capacity tiers first, then dedicated spare pools, then Hosted reserved nodes, then general Hosted. Introduce a "protected tier" flag to prevent escalation into low-priority Hosted pools for high-SLO tenants.
- Model-variant substitution matrix: store metadata per variant (expected latency distribution, quality score on evals, quantization artifacts) and only allow substitution if estimated quality delta < threshold. Provide automatic fallback ordering (e.g., Llama2-70B-int8 -> Llama2-70B-qat -> Llama2-30B-int8) and a conservative route for high-importance traffic.
- Backpressure and graceful degradation: when score falls below denial threshold, apply gradual rate-limiting + queueing and emit standardized error codes and reason strings so SDKs can surface UI/UX fallback.
- Observability and auditing: expose per-tenant escalation events, score breakdowns, pre/post-latency histograms, token-bucket utilization, and a routing decision trace ID that links to logs/trace. Add dashboards and alerting for unexpected escalation volumes.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Increased routing latency due to scoring; mitigate by optimizing for common case (cache high-score routes) and keeping scoring stateless where possible.
- Complexity in correctness (ensuring tenant accounting is robust in multi-region eventual consistency). We'll use conservative time windows and prefer rate limiting to "negative credits" in split-brain cases.
- Customer confusion: customers may see extra errors when credits are exhausted. Plan to provide clear docs, an opt-out flag for legacy behavior, and tooling in Console to visualize burst budgets.

Implementation plan (phases):
1) Spec + Simulation (2 wks): finalize score function, run closed-loop sims with historical traffic traces (notebooks linked).
2) Prototype (3 wks): implement scoring engine in routing layer behind feature flag, basic tenant token bucket in runtime. Add unit tests and e2e in staging.
3) Canaries (2 wks): enable for small subset of tenants, collect metrics and SLO impact.
4) Rollout + Controls (2 wks): Console controls, per-tenant opt-in, runbook updates.

Artifacts and links:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Capacity-Proxy+Routing+Guardrails
- Simulation notebook (internal GDrive): https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1XExampleSimNotebook
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821
- Observability dashboard prototype: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/route-safety/esc-control

Open questions:
- Exact scoring weights: need org decision on trade-off between cost vs. latency vs. quality. Propose default weights and allow tenant overrides.
- Billing model for purchased burst credits. Finance input required.
- SLO calculus for multi-hop region escalation (how to compute composite latency SLO impact).

Acceptance criteria:
- Routing layer implements score-based escalation and tenant token buckets behind flag.
- Simulation shows <1% of requests get denied at default thresholds in steady-state, and SLO regression <2% for canary tenants.
- Observability surfaces per-tenant escalation events and the score breakdown.
- Console has UI to view/modify burst budgets and opt-in/out flags.
comments: 2026-02-24 Aisha: Created ticket and initial spec. Uploaded sim traces to GDrive.
2026-02-28 Markus: Architecture review completed. Agreed on score vector components and that scoring should be cache-friendly. Action: implement prototype behind feature flag.
2026-03-03 Eng Leads: Decided to prioritise tenant-level token buckets + region penalty before complex model-variant gating to shorten lead time.
2026-03-07 Markus: Prototype PR opened (runtime/pull/4821). Basic scoring implemented; token bucket persisted in Redis with per-region shards.
2026-03-10 Performance: Simulation run (sim-2026-03-10) shows median route-selection latency +2ms, tail +18ms on worst-case scoring path. Need to cache positive routes for hot tenants.
2026-03-12 Security: Requested KMS review for token-bucket metadata stored with tenant IDs. Security review ticket created (ENG-24356).
